title: Young people are converting economic and technological uncertainty into local trust, purposeful work, and demand for co-authorship
source_unit: World Economic Forum, Youth Pulse 2026: Insights from the Next Generation for a Changing World
geography: Global youth perspectives from nearly 4,600 people ages 18–30 across 144 countries and territories and 489 locations

observations.period: 2026; youth economic outlook and personal stress

denominator.unit: nearly 4,600 young people ages 18–30 in the Youth Pulse study

inequality_concern.value: Nearly half identify deepening inequality as the leading economic trend shaping the future

financial_stress.value: Financial strain is identified as the foremost source of stress, and about half view inflation and instability as the greatest threats to their lives

resilience_response.value: Young people describe diversifying income, upskilling, entrepreneurship, and creative paths as responses to economic pressure

economic_meaning.value: Economic insecurity is shaping not only spending and work choices but also the kinds of institutions and futures young people consider credible

observations.method: World Economic Forum survey synthesis combining quantitative youth perspectives, qualitative reflections, and selected youth-led initiative examples across five dimensions.
observations.uncertainty: The publisher describes a global youth perspective sample rather than a probability sample of all young people; reported priorities and self-descriptions do not estimate population prevalence or causal effects of inflation, inequality, or entrepreneurship.
observations.subgroup: Young adults ages 18–30 across regions, with differences by geography, gender, socioeconomic position, education, and access to work, capital, and digital tools.
observations.counterinterpretation: Entrepreneurship and upskilling may reflect agency and opportunity as well as adaptation to weak formal pathways; they do not prove that young people prefer precarious or individualized solutions.

observations.period: 2026; purpose, flexibility, balance, and youth work expectations

career_values.value: Purpose, flexibility, and balance are prioritized ahead of traditional measures of career success across the report's youth-perspective synthesis

education_work_mismatch.unit: percent viewing education as a critical enabler while identifying a persistent mismatch between classroom learning and labor-market needs

pathway_demand.value: Young people call for practical, modular, employer-validated learning connected to emerging job markets

work_identity.value: Work is being evaluated through alignment among livelihood, well-being, purpose, and societal impact rather than pay or status alone

observations.method: World Economic Forum synthesis of survey responses and qualitative reflections on economic opportunity, education, work, and purpose.
observations.uncertainty: The reported preference pattern does not establish actual job choice, earnings, retention, or whether education reform would improve transitions; the 46% measure is a self-reported perception within the study sample.
observations.subgroup: Young students, workers, job seekers, entrepreneurs, and participants with different education-to-work pathways and labor-market conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Purpose and flexibility may be complements to secure pay and stable work rather than substitutes; respondents may express ideals that constraints prevent them from realizing.

observations.period: 2026; AI adoption, entry-level work, and skills conversion

regular_ai_use.unit: approximately percent using AI tools regularly, with another roughly one-third experimenting occasionally

entry_level_job_concern.unit: approximately percent fearing AI will reduce entry-level roles over the next three years

ai_education_gap.value: AI adoption is running ahead of formal training and meaningful work pathways

ai_inequality_risk.value: Young people describe a risk of a two-tier society in which routine junior tasks are automated while senior workers capture more of the gains

observations.method: World Economic Forum survey synthesis and youth-perspective reporting on AI use, education, work, and entry-level opportunity.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported AI use and perceived job risk are not measures of actual automation, employment displacement, productivity, or skill proficiency; the report's global comparisons may reflect unequal access and wording across contexts.
observations.subgroup: Young AI users, students, early-career workers, job seekers, employers, educators, and youth with unequal access to devices, connectivity, networks, and training.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI may create new entry pathways, augment junior work, and lower barriers to learning; perceived displacement can exceed realized labor-market effects.

observations.period: 2026; political trust, community leadership, and youth participation

local_trust.value: Trust is highest in community-level leaders and substantially lower for national political figures

trusted_leadership.value: Transparency and accountability are the most valued leadership traits

political_entry.value: More than one in three say they are likely to run for political office

proximity_legitimacy.value: For this youth perspective sample, legitimacy is associated more with proximity, accountability, and tangible delivery than with national status alone

observations.method: World Economic Forum comparative youth survey synthesis across political, social, and leadership questions.
observations.uncertainty: Trust comparisons depend on question wording, local political context, and self-reported perceptions; willingness to run for office is not actual participation or evidence that local leaders deliver better outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Young adults across local and national political contexts, including participants with different civic access, institutional experiences, and community roles.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community proximity may make leaders more visible rather than inherently more effective; low national trust can coexist with support for national institutions or policy action.

global_threat.value: Climate change ranks as the top global threat in the report's youth perspective synthesis

personal_threat.value: Climate change is viewed as the second greatest threat to young people's own lives after economic instability

youth_projects.unit: more than 120 youth-led climate projects catalogued as examples of action

climate_meaning.value: Climate action is framed as a precondition for prosperity rather than only a trade-off against affordability

observations.method: World Economic Forum survey synthesis combined with a catalogue of selected youth-led climate initiatives.
observations.uncertainty: The project examples are selected cases, not a representative inventory or causal evaluation; threat rankings measure perceived importance and do not predict future behavior or policy support.
observations.subgroup: Young people concerned about climate, youth-led organizations, community initiatives, educators, employers, and policy institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate concern can coexist with affordability constraints and political disagreement over policy instruments; catalogued projects may have unusual resources or visibility.

related_sources.claim: Public copy of the Youth Pulse 2026 report containing the methodology and key findings.
World Economic Forum summary of youth priorities, AI, education, climate, and community-level trust.
Official report landing page and publisher description.

boundary: This record adds a global youth-to-future route from cost pressure and inequality through work expectations, education mismatch, AI adoption, local trust, political participation, climate concern, and youth-led action. It preserves the World Economic Forum's publisher-survey and selected-case boundaries: these are youth perspectives and examples, not respondent-level behavioral traces, probability estimates for all young people, causal effects, or realized policy outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The public Youth Pulse 2026 report copy and World Economic Forum report summary were reviewed for sample frame, economic stress, purpose and work, AI adoption and entry-level job concern, local trust, political participation, climate rankings, and youth-led projects.
